text: "Hail, $playerName. I'm $PersonRank $personName, your service record with the $theFaction Navy is impressive. I've heard some flattering nicknames for you. How can we assist?"
"Transponder's recognized, $playerName. $theFaction has no quarrel with independent operators who've proven themselves reliable." Their eyes flick to a tactical display. "State your purpose."
"This is $PersonRank $personName of $theFaction Navy. Your IFF reads neutral. That can change very quickly, Captain, so let's keep this brief and professional."
"$theFaction Navy to hostile contact: we've fought worse than you in worse conditions. If you're not gone in sixty seconds, we'll add your wreckage to the rest."

"$PersonRank $personName, Alliance Navy." A measured pause. "You have tactical superiority. We're not disputing that. But Alliance Command tracks every engagement in this sector, and retaliation doctrine doesn't require us to win, just to make you memorable."
"Shouldn't you be running...?" The officer looks genuinely puzzled.

"Who the fu - Who is - What - I should kick your fucking ass, who is this?" There is a brief silence, cut short by the frantic sound of typing. "Ah, $playerName! I've notified the Department of Internal Security of your presence, leave immediately."

"Loyalty's a rare commodity out here, and you're fresh out. We've got no room for dual allegiances."

"That said, if you're serious about joining, resign from $theOtherCommissionFaction. And we'll gladly put your skills to use in $theFaction."

"I'm sorry, but you don't meet our criteria for receiving a commission. To put it plainly you're a wildcard, Commander. Shape up your outfit, purge the weak links, then come back. Until then, you're unfit for Draconis colors. However I've noted your request."

"Hmm, yes, you're a suitable candidate. Admiral August will be pleased. We're always short on manpower."

"Accepting a commission is a serious matter, however. You will be required to fight enemies of $theFaction. You'll be able to resign your commission at any time, though I don't imagine doing so would win you any friends."
"So, how about it? Still want to sign on?"
"Oath sworn. Welcome to the fold, Commander. Your IFF's updated - Draconis blue on your scope now."
"Anything else I can do for you?"

"Cold feet already?" $personName raises an eyebrow. "The Sector's full of fence-sitters who think twice when the guns start barking. Fafnir's ghosts don't suffer the hesitant, neither do we. Application withdrawn. If you grow a spine, our doors aren't barred... Yet."

"Resign? After we stamped your papers and handed you the keys to our armory? Commander, that's not how the Alliance works." $personFirstName pauses their typing to face you. "$TheFaction needs anyone it can get, and turning your back on us won't be forgotten."
$personFirstName sighs dramatically. "Fine. Resignation accepted, effective immediately. Your IFF's wiped, access codes revoked."
"Wise choice, Lieutenant. Knew you had the spine for it. Oath renewed - no hard feelings, just hard lessons."

Fleet Admiral August has personally recognized your contributions to the Alliance. Joint Command has extended full access to military stockpiles and forward operating bases, and even the most security-conscious AIO liaison officers no longer shadow your movements. Alliance Citizens across Fafnir regard you as one of their own - a rare distinction for anyone who didn't endure the Reunification.

Alliance officials have come to regard you as a reliable partner rather than a convenient asset. Port authorities process your docking requests without the usual security theater, and patrol captains are more likely to offer assistance than demand transponder logs. The gratitude of Joint Command translates to meaningful access to military-grade hardware.

Your reputation has reached the attention of mid-level Alliance commanders, several of whom have noted your reliability in official dispatches. System patrols treat your $shipOrFleet as a known quantity rather than a potential threat, and port authorities extend courtesies typically reserved for Alliance-flagged vessels.

Alliance commanders have begun to take note of your activities - favorably, if cautiously. In practice, this means access to surplus military equipment and fewer pointed questions from patrol captains. The institutional paranoia born from the civil war hasn't faded entirely, but you've earned the benefit of the doubt.

To Alliance officials, you're simply another independent operator - neither a threat nor an asset worth cultivating. This is, by local standards, a reasonable position to occupy. The DDA's history has left its leadership wary of outsiders, but not hostile without cause.

Something in your record has drawn scrutiny from Alliance security. Port authorities process your requests with deliberate slowness, and patrol commanders run your transponder against watchlists more often than strictly necessary. You're not unwelcome, but you're certainly not trusted.

Joint Command has flagged your $shipOrFleet as a potential security concern. Port officials find reasons to deny docking requests, and patrol captains interpret their rules of engagement generously when your drives light up on their scopes. The Alliance hasn't declared you an enemy - but they've stopped pretending you might be a friend.

Alliance patrols are authorized to engage your $shipOrFleet on sight. Markets under DDA control deny you access, and any incident involving your vessels is treated as confirmation of hostile intent. Whatever goodwill you might have once possessed has been thoroughly exhausted.

The Alliance has classified you as an active threat to sector stability. Your name circulates in Joint Command briefings alongside pirates, warlords, and other enemies of the fragile peace August built from the ashes of civil war. No patrol captain will hesitate to add your $shipOrFleet to the long list of threats the DDA has ground to dust.

Joint Command regards your $shipOrFleet as one more hostile element in a sector that produces them endlessly. Alliance captains have standing orders to engage and destroy - the same orders they've executed against countless threats since the Reunification. You are not special. You are simply next.

The Alliance views your growing power as an existential threat to everything the Reunification preserved. Somewhere in Joint Command, planners are assembling a task force with your colonies marked for pacification. The DDA has survived civil war, corporate predation, and worse. They do not intend to let you succeed where those threats failed.

text:
"I remember a raid on Athebyne's supply depots, some cycles ago. We were running low on everything - fuel, munitions, pilots. Lieutenant Reyes - solid flyer, came up through the reserves - took a squadron of Grumiums on what should've been a suicide run. Six wings, loaded heavy, against fortified emplacements and interceptor screens."

"Lumbered in like cargo haulers. Reyes lost half his wing before they even lined up the shot. But the ones that made it through? Dropped their payload right into the heart of the depot. Chain reactions lit up the night side of the planet. We got the resupply we needed to hold the line another month."

"Reyes brought three back. Got a commendation posthumously - caught a missile on the egress. The Grumium's no hero's ride. Slow, ugly work. But if it kills, it serves. And sometimes, that's all you need."

A brief pause as the transfer finalizes.

"Commander."

"I remember a raid on Athebyne's supply depots, some cycles ago. We were running low on everything - fuel, munitions, pilots. Lieutenant Reyes - solid flyer, came up through the reserves - took a squadron of Grumiums on what should've been a suicide run. "Reyes brought three back. Got a commendation posthumously - caught a missile on the egress. The Grumium's no hero's ride. Slow, ugly work. But if it kills, it serves. And sometimes, that's all you need."

A brief pause as the transfer finalizes.

"Commander."

"Most people look at her now and see a relic - ill fit for modern combat. But I remember when she was all we had.

Third week of the siege at Athebyne orbital. My flagship had taken a reactor hit, and I transferred my flag to the Resolute - an Alruba. We had six of them left in the picket line, facing down twice our number.

The captain - Walker, good officer - kept us between the troop transports and their missile boats. Took hits that would've gutted a Thuban. The armor held. Barely. By the time relief arrived, we'd lost three Alrubas, but the transports made it through.

Walker didn't. Reactor breach on the final push.

The Alruba's not fast. Not elegant. But she's honest. And doesn't quit until she's a debris field. Sometimes that's enough."

A brief pause as the data finalizes.

"That'll be all, Commander."

"The Shaobi. The Marines' favorite toy. Command didn't want to build her - too specialized, too expensive. But the Marines made their case, and somehow, it stuck.

I'll admit, I didn't see the value. Not at first.

Then came the boarding operation at Ring-Port - back when it was still under separatist control. We needed to take the station intact, and orbital bombardment wasn't an option. That meant Marines. Lots of them.

The Shaobi-class Warhound led the assault. Two hundred Marines, full combat load, deployed in under twenty minutes. They hit three docking points simultaneously - precision insertion, no warning.

The captain - Major Hartley, Marine Corps - she coordinated the whole thing from the Warhound's bridge. Ship-to-boarding-craft comms, real-time tactical updates, fire support from the gunship's turrets. It wasn't just a carrier - it was a forward command post with engines.

We took Ring-Port in six hours. Minimal casualties. Hartley got a medal. The Warhound got a reputation.

The Shaobi's not a fleet carrier. She's not meant to be. But if you need boots on a station or a hostile ship, she'll get them there - and bring them home.

Sometimes that's worth more than another fighter wing."

A pause.

"The Alliance chose well with you, Commander. Transfer authorized."

"A carrier escort strictly speaking. Compromised sensors to save weight and meet project requirements. Command signed off on it because she was never meant to operate independently.

That became a problem during the push on Athebyne's outer stations. We had the Milwaukee - assigned to screen the Io's carrier group. Standard formation, textbook deployment. Then the carrier's sensor array took a hit from long-range fire. Partial failure - enough to briefly shunt the datalink, not enough to justify pulling back.

The Milwaukee was supposed to provide missile support. But with the carrier's sensors degraded and her own array already limited, she couldn't get a clean firing solution on anything beyond visual range. Captain Holt - had a ship full of ordnance and nothing to shoot at.

So he did what the ship wasn't designed to do: he moved in close. Uncomfortably close.

The Milwaukee took more hits in that engagement than any other ship in the group. Lost two crew compartments, vented half her missile reserves in an ammunition cook off. But the carrier stayed operational, and the screen held."

Your sensors officer glances back at you, eyebrows raised. Authorization codes transmitted.

"Until next time, Commander."

"Even while it serves it's considered a 'prototype'. Armored like a battleship, just fast enough to keep up with cruiser squadrons. On paper, she's perfect. In practice? A damned miracle - when she works.

At end of the war had four Juzas in active service. The Jericho was flagship for the third battle group - my XO's command. Fleet engagement near Athebyne's inner belt. Standard line battle, cruiser-on-cruiser.

Then the Jericho's flux regulators spiked. Total system failure - her shields dropped, her weapons went cold. A paperweight in the middle of a firing line.

Her chief engineer - man named Nowak, stubborn bastard - he rerouted power through the secondary grid, bypassed the safeties, and brought the flux system back online in under three minutes. A miracle to put it bluntly.

By the time the Jericho came back, she'd taken fourteen direct hits. Her armor held. Barely. Nowak kept her running for another six hours before the system burned out for good. We won that engagement.

The Juza's temperamental. High-maintenance. But if you've got a crew that knows her quirks, she'll hold the line when everything else breaks."

A brief silence followed by an authorization code transmission.

"Authorization granted."

"I've heard the jokes - "by the time she arrives, the war's over." The crews call her the 'Late Arrival.'

An anecdote: Textbook carrier doctrine. Three battlegroups were to warp directly into the fight. The Alwaid's group? Delayed by a drive malfunction - forty minutes late to the fight.

By the time they arrived, we'd lost Heaven's Axiom and half her escort. The Diligence was burning, venting atmosphere from six hull breaches. We were fifteen minutes from a full retreat.

Then the Eternity translated in-system. Two hundred and sixty fighters. Every torpedo tube loaded. She didn't win the battle herself - but she ended it. The enemy scattered. We held the orbitals.

The Alwaid's slow. But when she gets there, she brings everything."

The faintest pause.

"It's yours."

"Four cycles ago, a Pather raiding flotilla entered Kori's orbital space in coordination with a surface sabotage operation. The intent was to occupy our response force long enough for the ground teams to finish their work. The Covenant was in the patrol rotation.

Vasile, her commander, took her through the center of the formation. Struck their lead ship at speed, engaged the second at close range, and repositioned between the flotilla and their egress vector before their command element had processed what had happened. The aft section took heavy damage. Prioritized forward coverage with the rear mount. But even so, the flotilla broke. The surface teams lost their extraction window.

The after-action report was four pages. Three and a half of them were just damage assessments. The remaining half-page described his tactical reasoning in language I found adequate but incomplete. He did not mention that the Covenant's approach vector was inconsistent with any evasive option - that closing at that speed, on that bearing, was not a response to the engagement. It was a conclusion he had reached before the engagement began.

He is a precise man. His logs are immaculate. I do not think the imprecision was accidental."

A silence. Although not long.

"Take good care of her, Commander. The Alliance has few enough of these."

"A capable hull." He keys something on the console. "Authorization complete."

A brief pause as the transfer finalizes.

"Good hunting, Commander."

"The Office has been patient. We watch until we understand the shape of a problem. We understand yours."

"What you're using draws attention the Alliance cannot afford. We maintain relationships that depend on this corner of the Sector staying unremarkable. He glances at his drink. "A commission is available, if you'd prefer a structural solution to an accounting one. The Office prefers operators inside the framework rather than adjacent to it. But in my experience, people find our arrangement preferable."

"The assessment cycle resumes where it paused."

He turns his glass slowly.

"You've been inside it already. $aio_months. The inspection fleet that diverted, the quarterly assessments that never materialised." He waits - not for your response, but to let you count the incidents. "Those weren't coincidence."

"The cycle resumes. The outcomes it produces are not accidents. Most people don't notice the difference until it's academic."

"To not be here."

"Specifically - for your operation to stop generating signals that require a response. The arrangement creates that condition. Your cores stay in their housings; the Office stops noticing them. Both parties have less work."

"The Office doesn't want your loyalty. It wants your noise to stop."

"When I leave, it changes. Three words, maximum. Procedural."

"We... um... don't have a flag for... what you just did..."

An awkward pause follows, one that lasts a little too long while the captain logs something out of sight. "Well, we have a flag for it now."

"There is no precedent in Alliance regs for denying access via unsanctioned transit vectors. I've checked. We're aware you're here."

"Conduct yourself accordingly. We'll be watching."

text:
The beacon is old. Domain-pattern, pitted gray by cycles of particle wash, its solar collectors long since scoured blind. Its transmitter is not old at all - the loop is Alliance-issue.

"NAVIGATIONAL HAZARD. Particle flux beyond this marker exceeds survivable tolerance for unshielded hulls. Turn back."

"The Fafnir system is closed to unauthorized traffic by standing order of the Draconis Defense Alliance. Vessels attempting transit without current approach data will be intercepted. Consider this your notification."

Underneath it, on a subcarrier nobody troubled to strip out, the buoy's original signal is still running. Survey-standard, pre-Collapse, patient as anything.

"...unresolved anomaly. Origin unknown. Do not approach. Do not approach. Do not..."

Your comms officer holds the second channel a moment longer than necessary, then closes it.
notes: Fafnir approach beacon, hyperspace. Placed by XLII_System.ensureRiftBeacon(). Outscores vanilla beaconOpenDialog via the score:100 on $XLII_riftBeacon, which is set on the beacon entity memory. Reuses vanilla beaconLeave option handler.

text:
The particle count climbs before your sensors will admit what they are looking at.

The radiation ahead is not weather your helm can read - it is high-energy wash with no coherent structure, and the instruments render it as noise the whole way down. Combat readiness is already bleeding off the boards.

Your navigation officer lets the returns run a while longer than the plot needs.

"We could try to push through. I'd rather not say how far." A pause. "But traffic goes through here, Captain. Regularly. Somebody is definitely selling the approach."

"I've heard Tri-Tachyon runs couriers into Fafnir often. And the pirates have been running guns to Ring-Port for thirty cycles now. Neither of them is doing it blind." The plot goes dark. "Could ask in the right bar?"
notes: One-shot beat on first Rift crossing. Fired from XLII_RiftTerrainPlugin.maybeShowFirstEntryDialog() via RuleBasedInteractionDialogPluginImpl("XLII_RiftEntry") on the player fleet. MEM_RIFT_FIRST_ENTRY_DONE is set by the terrain plugin before opening, not here.

text:
There's a man at the docking office threshold with the stillness of someone who has been there longer than you've been in system. He has no rank markings and no reason to be waiting here that isn't you.

He doesn't offer anything except a brief glance at your vessel registration tag, then to you - then down to his datapad.

"Transit log confirmed... Credentials reconciled... Done."

He gives a nod and turns away. The conversation appears to be complete.

text:
He scans your transponder without preamble and checks something off on his slate.

"Shipment's in." He doesn't look up. "Good."

He marks it in the system. No receipt. No signature. Just a note in whatever ledger Ring-Port keeps. You're in their books.

He goes back to the manifests. You're done here.

text:
Closer inspection reveals a skeletal lattice of military emplacements: gun batteries fused into slag, sensor arrays crumpled like paper, armored hab-modules cracked open to vacuum.

Hazard stripes still clings stubbornly to the hull plating beneath layers of micrometeorite scarring and weapons burns.

Faint emergency strobes - long dead - mark the positions where XLII Fleet gun crews once waited, cycle after cycle, for an enemy that never came through.

text:
Your salvage teams force the frost-sealed airlock of the primary command module. Flashlights sweep across derelict consoles and drifting slats.

Your Ops Chief breaks the silence "$PlayerSirOrMadam, archives are intact. Something to do with the '42nd Signal Corps' relays, seems untouched since the ring cracked."

A brief moment as they interface with the databank.

"Gate Vigil logs recovered - Rear Admiral S. Surher's final entry - mid-bombardment."

"There are more fragments here. Relocation orders to Kori, personnel lists. Permission to extract the full cache?"

Your officers wait for your orders, the soft whine of data recovery filling the bridge.

script: AddTextSmall "Log Fragment 1 - XLII Signal Corps Standing Order 224-19" highlight
text:
"Cycle 47 pre-Alliance. Auth: Capt. Emil August, forwarded through Corps Command."

"'All Signal Corps detachments are hereby detached from line-of-battle duties and assigned to permanent perimeter security and monitoring of Fafnir Gate structure. Primary objective: detect and report any unauthorized hyperspace transit attempt. Secondary objective: prevent physical access by non-cleared personnel.

This assignment is non-negotiable. Resources will be reallocated accordingly.

Endorsement appended by Lt. Cmdr. J. Halvorsen, Signal Corps:

"Understood the strategic logic on paper. Still feels like punishment duty. We're bleeding hull plating at Athebyne's Lagrange points while half the corps sits on cold alloy watching a ring that hasn't twitched since the Collapse. August must know something we don't. Or he's finally lost it."'

script: AddTextSmall "Log Fragment 2 - Field Engineering Log, Attempt Series 12-47" highlight
text:
"Cycle 49 pre-Alliance. Auth: Lt. Mara Velas, Field Engineering Lead."

"'Attempt 47 concluded 03:14 shipboard. Full power shunt through primary manifold coupling. Ring returned to quiescent state within 0.8 seconds. No aperture formation, no phase excursion, no manifold breach.

Same result as Attempt 46. And 45. And every attempt back to 12.

However: return signal consistent across all attempts. Three discrete hyperwave pulses, 1.7-second spacing, identical modulation envelope. Subcarrier contains structured data we cannot yet parse. It responds to our probe strength - louder input yields louder reply.

It is not an echo. It is a handshake.

Recommendation: cease active attempts until we can fabricate better decoding hardware. Morale note: crew has started calling the anomaly 'the patient one.' Not sure I like the nickname.'"

script: AddTextSmall "Log Fragment 3 - Redeployment Directive, Eyes-Only" highlight
text:
"Cycle 51 pre-Alliance. Auth: Adm. Emil August, countersigned AIO precursor cell."

"'Effective immediately: all Signal Corps assets under designation 'Gatewatch' are to cease operations at Fafnir Gate and redeploy subsurface, Kori primary grid, reference Alpha-7 / Theta-9.

New primary objective: secure, stabilize, and establish interface protocols with Domain-era megastructure; codeword designation: [LONGSIGHT].

All previous Gate monitoring logs are to be archived under maximum encryption and physically transferred to Kori vault. No further active interrogation of the Gate permitted. Demolition charges remain on standby per prior order.

Personal addendum, August: "The answers are under Kori. That is where the war will be decided now."'

AddStoryPoints 1
BeginMission BlindEyeQuestMission
$global.XLII_gateLogRead = true
text:
"Cycle 52 pre-Alliance. Auth: precursor cell, later designated Alliance Intelligence Office."

"'Signal Corps detachment Gatewatch formally stood down. Surviving personnel and technical assets folded into new standing formation: Alliance Intelligence Section (provisional) under Rear Admiral S. Surher's oversight.

Mission parameters redefined: - Acquisition, integration, and operational employment of [LONGSIGHT]-derived computational systems. - Evaluation and controlled implementation of AI-core augmentation protocols previously prohibited under Sector norms. - Protection of all related programs from external compromise (Hegemony, Persean League, Tri-Tachyon, Luddic elements). - Elimination or reorientation of personnel who represent unacceptable risk to operational security.

From this cycle forward, the Section answers only to unified command authority. Taboos are suspended for the duration of the emergency - which is now declared permanent.

Final line, unsigned but cipher-matched to August: "You are no longer watchers. You are keepers. And you shall keep what must never be loosed upon the Sector... or what must be loosed only by our hand."'

They tap the console once more, locking the slate.

"Whatever [LONGSIGHT] actually is... it didn't come through the Gate. It was already here. And it's been talking to them."

A beat of silence on the bridge.

"Orders, Captain?"

Stellar Array Alpha - one of three stations spaced evenly around this orbit, each of them holding its face to Fafnir.

Edge-on it does not exist. Your sensor officer finds it by the hole it leaves in the starfield - a band of absent light eleven kilometres across and, by the return, no thicker than a few hundred molecules.

It keeps its angle as you close. Nothing in the motion suggests machinery.
notes: Stellar Array Alpha. score:1000 overrides vanilla stellarMirrorOpenDialog, which matches $tag:stellar_mirror at score 1 - without the bump the two tie and the engine picks between them at random. Options come from XLII_MirrorSurveyOptions so the same rule serves surveyed and unsurveyed states. Approach text must stay order-independent: the player can reach any array first. Reference the three-array geometry freely (it is on the system chart) but never anything learned at another array.

text:
Stellar Array Bravo rides this orbit a third of a turn from Alpha and a third again from Charlie, on the fixed bearing the chart gives all three.

Eleven kilometres of foil, and no way onto it. No docking collar, no berthing spar, no service gantry, no hatch on any surface your scopes can resolve.

Whatever built this array did not expect anyone to come back to it.

text:
Stellar Array Charlie, third of the stations on this orbit, matching the survey figures for Alpha and Bravo to within the error of the instrument.

It takes your sensor officer several minutes to say what is wrong with the returns, because the problem is not something present in them.

The hull is clean. Not maintained - clean. Thirty cycles of war in this system, and the surface reads as though nothing has ever been near it.

text:
Your team spends four hours on the collector spine. Your Ops Chief reads the returns twice before speaking.

"It's not a reflector, $PlayerSirOrMadam. There's no focal assembly, and there's nothing downrange to reflect onto. It's aimed at the star, and the star is the only thing it has ever been aimed at."

They set the slate down.

"And it's drawing. I can't tell you from what. Thermal's dead, no plasma tap, no corona intercept - it isn't a shunt, before you ask, I checked that first. But the collection budget on this one array runs to eleven figures and I've nowhere to put the decimal."

A pause.

"Historians called these mirrors. Whoever wrote that never came out here."
notes: Fragment 1 of 3 - the arithmetic does not close, and the object is not what the record says it is.

text:
Six hours on the spine and your team finds no way inside. What they find instead is a housekeeping channel, unencrypted, broadcasting to nobody.

"Alignment log, $PlayerSirOrMadam. It corrects itself. Sub-arcsecond, continuous, and it has been doing it without interruption for as far back as the buffer runs."

Your Ops Chief scrolls, and keeps scrolling.

"Last correction was fourteen minutes ago."

A beat.

"There's no crew. Nothing seems to have docked here since the end of their war. I had the Sustainment archive queried on the way out - there is no maintenance contract for these arrays, there has never been a maintenance contract for these arrays, and Acquisitions has a form for that. It's the one you file when the asset does not require servicing."
notes: Fragment 2 of 3 - something has been maintaining these for centuries and it is not the Alliance.

text:
Your team walks the full face and reports no impact scarring. No micrometeorite pitting. No weapons burns.

"The Gate took a beating and the Gate wasn't even a target, $PlayerSirOrMadam. This thing sat through the entire war."

Your Ops Chief has the fleet archive open.

"Athebyne's bombardment groups transited inside weapons range of this array on eleven recorded occasions. Nobody fired. Not a warning shot, not a ranging round. It isn't on anyone's target list, and I can't find the order that took it off."

They hesitate over the last of it.

"One more thing. Whatever this array does, it doesn't do it at a constant rate. The housekeeping buffer keeps the peaks - it ramps when something downrange calls for it, and holds until whatever that is has had its fill. The longest on record runs seventy-two hours."

Nobody on the bridge asks which seventy-two hours.
notes: Fragment 3 of 3 - untouched by the war, and drawing hardest while Athebyne burned. Phrasing of the throttle beat is deliberately self-contained; it cannot assume the player has run Alpha's survey and knows the array draws at all.

text:
Comms flags an inbound hail on an Alliance military band. No fleet on the scope. No origin marker.

The voice is unhurried, and slightly bored.

"Vessel at close station on the collector array. You are logged. Survey activity in this orbit is prohibited under standing instruction - reference is not provided. Confirm you are departing."

A pause, exactly as long as courtesy requires.

"Your inquiry is noted."
notes: Fires once, on whichever array is surveyed first. The Office logs the transgression rather than acting on it.

text: No hail this time. Whatever is listening has already made its position clear, and does not appear to feel the need to repeat itself.
notes: Second and third surveys - the watcher is still there, it simply has nothing to add.

text:
"Noted."

The link cuts.

"Which instruction?"

A silence. Not hesitation - a decision.

"The instruction is standing. That is the whole of what I have."

The link cuts.
notes: The operator is not being cagey. There is no reference to give, and nobody in the chain has found that strange for a long time.

text:
The channel stays open for eleven seconds. Then: "Understood."

It closes.

Three sets of returns on one plot. Your Ops Chief runs the vectors out and does not need long.

"They don't converge on a planet, $PlayerSirOrMadam. They converge under one."

The intersect resolves kilometres beneath Kori's ice, well below the shipyards, in a volume that appears on no Alliance survey chart at any classification your fleet is cleared to read.

"The Gate cache had a codeword for whatever's down there."

A pause.

"It didn't mention that the thing needs feeding."
notes: Variant shown when the player has read the Fafnir Gate logs - the crew can name what the arrays are feeding.

text:
Three sets of returns on one plot. Your Ops Chief runs the vectors out and does not need long.

"They don't converge on a planet, $PlayerSirOrMadam. They converge under one."

The intersect resolves kilometres beneath Kori's ice, well below the shipyards, in a volume that appears on no Alliance survey chart at any classification your fleet is cleared to read.

"So it all goes there. Three arrays' worth, into a hole under their own headquarters."

A pause.

"I'd very much like to know what's using it."
notes: Variant shown without the Gate logs - same discovery, no name to put to it.

text:
Your Ops Chief is still working. Something in their posture changes.

"It doesn't balance."

They turn the plot. "Whatever's down there is taking a fraction. A large fraction - but a fraction. You cannot siphon on this scale and not shed the remainder somewhere, and the remainder is the larger number."

"It's been called a hyperspace anomaly since before the Alliance," your sensor officer says. "It's in the pilot notes. There's a defense doctrine built on it."

Nobody finishes the thought aloud.

The Rift is not weather. The Rift is exhaust - and the machinery that makes it has been running, without interruption or supervision, since long before anyone in Fafnir was born.

Which leaves one question, and your Ops Chief has the good sense not to ask it. What becomes of the wall, if the machinery ever stops.
notes: Sets $global.XLII_mirrorSurveyComplete - dormant hook for later AIO/Iron Moth dialogue referencing the player having worked this out.

text:
The bar's wall screens, regardless of what channel, flicker and tune to the anniversary feed again, archival footage worn soft at the edges, the Fleet Admiral August's voice flattened by two generations of re-encoding.

It recalls patriotic accounts from the war, thanks to the sacrifices of the Itoron people, their bravery and their unwavering loyalty to a better tomorrow.

"...As my predecessor, Samuel Harrows, once said: 'We will answer this butchery with everything Itoron has ever built, and we will answer it until no convoy, no worker, no citizen of this world need ever again look to the stars and wonder if today is the day they burn.' And I will reiterate our great pledge made good: the sector, nor Athebyne, dare not threaten us again."

Nobody in the room is watching the footage per se. They're watching each other watch it. A dockhand near the taps sets down her glass in something that isn't quite attention and isn't quite indifference. When the reel finishes and turns back to its original channels, a few patrons raise their glasses without being told to.

text: You lift your glass along with the rest of the room. Nobody comments on it, but the dockhand allows you the smallest of nods before turning back to her drink. Whatever brought you to Fafnir, tonight the reel makes you one of them, for as long as it loops.

You keep your eyes on the room instead of the screen. The reverence is real enough - nobody here is performing it for your benefit - but it sits oddly next to the ration crates stacked by the door and a price board somebody's chalked over twice this week. Whatever the broadcast is selling, the room isn't buying quite as evenly as it looks.
You leave them to it. Whatever the broadcast is selling, you didn't come here to buy it.

text:
Kori's dockside bar keeps its heat turned up past what the rest of the station allows, a small mercy for crews just off an eighteen-hour shift in yard cold that gets into the joints and stays there. A knot of orbitalworks techs has claimed the corner table, ledger open, counting credits into two piles.

"$playerName," one of them says without looking up. "Good timing. We've got a pool running on which hull rolls off the floor first this week."

She taps the ledger. Two names are chalked at the top, odds scrawled underneath in a hand that's had steadier days.

You wave off the pool and buy the table a round instead. It buys you twenty minutes of unguarded shop talk about fabrication tolerances and a supervisor nobody at the table likes, which is worth more to you than the pool would have been.
You leave them to their ledger and find a quieter table.

text:
Athebyne's dockside bar keeps its lighting low and its air recyclers loud, habits from a planet where privacy used to mean something. Tonight the noise curdles fast. A dome-shift crew three drinks past sensible has taken the corner table, and one of them - forearm scarred where a suit seal failed years back - stands up on her chair to be heard over the recyclers.

"Rights." She turns the word over like she's checking it for cracks. "We have rights. Same as anyone lucky enough to be born on the right side of the bombardment. Same as anyone Itoron didn't bury and call it rescue."

Two Internal Security troopers hold the door, carbines slung across their chests the way soldiers stand in a room that might turn on them. The taller one starts across the floor. He doesn't get three steps before she turns on him instead.

"You forgot we were people somewhere back on Itoron," she says, and the bar's gone quiet enough that everyone hears it. "We'll remind you the only way you still listen."

She puts the glass into his face before his rifle clears its sling. A second miner drives his shoulder into the other trooper, and by the time either of them gets a weapon up, half the bar is already on its feet. You are three meters from the middle of it.
options:
1:XLII_bar_athebyne_side_security:Wade in on Internal Security's side
2:XLII_bar_athebyne_side_crowd:Pull the miners clear of Security

notes: Reworked this session: security-vs-crowd riot replacing the dosimeter joke/round/leave flavor scene. Centerpiece line is inspired by an Expanse quote (dehumanization answered with violence) but rewritten from scratch into the agitator's own words rather than dropped in verbatim. Internal Security personnel are armed troopers (carbines, not batons) per author note - the DDA is a stratocracy with no separate civilian police, so its Athebyne enforcement presence is soldiers, not officers. Passed a banned.md revision pass (cut a stock simile, two negation-formula constructions, a truism-style ending line - see starsector-writing skill).

text: You put your shoulder into the man still swinging and pin him against the bulkhead before the trooper's rifle finishes coming level. Cuffing the woman takes two of you; she keeps talking the whole time, past the troopers, past you, at whoever in the bar is still listening. By the time Internal Security has binds on four dome-shift miners, nobody at the bar is looking at anyone else. The trooper you helped lowers his weapon, gives you a short nod, and goes back to his prisoner.
notes: Backing Internal Security against the crowd: +rep XLII_draconis, -rep pirates.

text: You get an arm under the man on the floor and haul him clear of a rifle butt aimed at his ribs. The woman is still shouting the same line when you shove her through the service hatch, aimed now at nobody but the closing door. Behind you, a trooper is shouting for backup into a comm nobody dockside is in a hurry to answer. By the time reinforcements arrive, the corner table is empty, the miners are gone into Athebyne's warrens where no patrol goes without a squad, and the bar is full of witnesses who all remember nothing.

text: You don't wait to find out how thorough Internal Security gets once it starts asking names. Two blocks and one shuttle ride later, you're at a different dockside bar - quieter, a different bartender, no idea what happened at the last one and no particular interest in asking.

text: You stay at the bar and let it happen around you. It's over inside two minutes: Internal Security moves like soldiers who've done this before, because they have. Four dome-shift miners go out in zip-strips, one of them not moving under his own power, another with a rifle stock-mark already swelling above his eye. The woman keeps talking right up until they get her through the airlock. Nobody meets your eyes on the way out, including the bartender, who pours you another without being asked and waves off payment.

text:
Vorium's officers' mess doubles as the nearest thing the moon has to a bar, once ship's law expects everyone off-duty to be somewhere. A table of patrol crew, still half in their vac gear, are working through their third round and a familiar complaint.

"Third convoy this month out to Tiamat," one of them says, dragging a thumb across a data-slate. "Third time Ring-Port's scouts get a look at us before we get a look at them."

"Write it up," someone else says, not looking up. "Command loves paperwork on things they already know."

They notice you before you've decided whether to sit.

text: You pull up a chair and trade convoy stories, yours a little more embellished than theirs. Nobody calls you on it. By the time the round's gone dry, the data-slate's been forgotten under a beer ring, and the complaint about Ring-Port has turned into simple griping about the escort schedule, which is at least a complaint with an end date.

You buy the table a round and let them vent without adding your own war stories to the pile. It's not much, but the officer with the data-slate looks up long enough to actually thank you, which by the sound of things before you sat down, isn't something Command manages very often.
Some things aren't yours to fix. You leave them to their complaint and their third round.

text:
Two off-duty officers have claimed the end of the bar, voices pitched low in the particular register of people who think they're being quiet. You catch it anyway.

"...they told them the sweep on the Gate wreck was complete. But nobody ever went back to confirm it."

"So the records are still sitting out there?"

"If nobody torched it, sure. Command has had ages to send a team back and finish the job properly - they haven't... Draw your own conclusions, man."

The second officer says something too quiet to catch. The first laughs, short and humorless, before they both clock the bartender within earshot and they hush themselves.

You drift a step closer, nursing your drink and angling for better acoustics.

"...if it's still out there," the quieter one says, "half the Signal Corps roster from that era has been reassigned to Ladon. That's not the kind of oversight anybody wants to explain."

"Well hey, at least it's not ours to explain," the first replies, and that's where it ends - a hand on a shoulder, a change of subject and a particular feelings of finality.
Whatever it is, it isn't your business to overhear. You let the rest go and turn back to your own table.

text:
He does not answer at once. Somewhere behind him a hatch cycles and someone says a number twice.

"Well Ring-Port runs itself now. August has people for the paperwork." A pause. "I'm told that's a compliment..."

He looks at the pickup.

"Ask me properly and I'll come."

"Then I'll requisition my own transfer - faster that way."

The line stays open a moment longer than it needs to.

"I'm no use to you idle, Commander. I'll be aboard."

text: "Understood." No inflection. "The posting isn't going anywhere."

He picks up on the first ping. Behind him, his own bridge - quieter than yours, and arranged like he expects to be there a while.

"Commander!"
OR
He picks up on the first ping. His wardroom, mid-briefing. Three of his officers are enjoying it more than he is. He sends them out with a look and turns back to the pickup.

"Commander. Good timing, as it happens."

He answers from somewhere in his own engineering spaces, with the sound of a running plant behind him.

"One moment." A hand gesture and the noise drops by half. "Commander?"
OR

"Commander, what do you need?"

His quarters, with the door open behind him - which the crew have worked out is deliberate.

"Commander. Come in, so to speak."

text:

"Hello, Commander."

"Commander, just a second..."

He sits in your wardroom, where he is being extremely careful not to give anybody an order.

"Commander. I was beginning to think I had been forgotten about."

You find him in cargo control, where he is checking a rotation that is not his to check. The rating on watch seems glad of the company.

"Commander."

"Yes, Commander?"

text:
He is in the observation blister on the spine, where the crew go when they want to not be found. He does not seem embarrassed to be caught at it.

"Commander." He makes no attempt to look like he was doing something else. "I am told idleness is good for the constitution."
OR
He is in the galley, at an hour when nobody else is in it, working through a stack of freight manifests he brought aboard himself.

"Commander?"
OR
Somewhere in the aft passages. He is learning your ship by walking it end to end, which he has been doing for serval days.

"Commander. I think the frame numbering is inconsistent aft of the mid-section..."
OR
Korrin sits in a borrowed corner of the mess, a datapad, and a cup of something that went cold a while ago.

"Commander!"
OR
He is sitting in on the navigation watch, saying nothing and missing less. He steps away when he sees the light.

"Commander?"

Korrin doesn't wait for you to bring it up.

text:
He has the salvage manifest open, and he has clearly had it open for some time.

"Commander. The construction of that survey ship - the fabrication marks."

He turns the slate around so you can see it, then seems to think better of it and sets it down.

"They are ours. Not similar. Ours. Same tooling pattern the yards at Kori still run."

"I would like to know how that is possible before I write it down anywhere."
notes: Domain thread opener. Queued by KorrinObserver on discovering a derelict survey ship.

text:
"Standardized across the Domain, yes. But..."

He does not sound argumentative about it moreso like a man checking his work.

"Eleven thousand manifests in the Kori archive. I have read most of them."

He takes a breath and continues.

"With all due respect, we are one of the only polities that can make anything not burdened by Domain-era encryption. But the question is how, and why does it match so closely with Domain spec...?"

He does not answer his own questions, he just sits with them a moment.

"You may well be right. I would like you to be."
notes: No reputation - a fair answer he has already considered himself.

text:
"No. I had already decided that, which is the part that concerns me."

A brief pause.

"I'd like to think I'm quite thorough, Commander. But this is the first thing I have chosen not to file."
notes: Rep: siding with him against his own filing habit. The arc beat.

text:
He has the port authority's atmospheric assay open - the public one, handed out free at the customs desk.

"Sulphur compounds, refining by-products, actinides at a level the sheet calls manageable. Two hundred cycles of meeting quotas did that."

He sets the slate down.

"I asked a bonded secretary downstairs what her office held on a system called Fafnir. She was helpful. She asked me to spell it, and then she asked me if I was sure."

That gets a short laugh out of him.

"So I have given up on the large questions and I would like a small one answered. Do they go outside? There are more people under that sky than I have ever seen counted on a single document. Nothing in here tells me whether a man on Chicomoztoc walks to work in the open air."
notes: Hegemony thread. Queued by KorrinObserver on docking at Chicomoztoc. The question is deliberately unglamorous - his bible has him asking about weather and what people eat, and the Athebyne resonance lands harder for never being said.

options: 10:korrin_heg_chico_outside:They go outside, just not for long

text:
"That is the first thing anybody has told me about this place that I could not have read from here."

He writes it down, and seems more pleased with it than the sentence obviously justifies.

"Twenty minutes and a filter mask, at a guess. Sounds a lot like somewhere back home..."

"I had assumed the answer would be no. It is pleasant to be wrong about something before lunch."

"Sealed end to end. So the sky is rare commodity."

He turns that over for a moment.

"Then the assay is not a warning. It is a weather report for a place nobody stands in, printed because somebody's charter says it has to be."

He puts the slate away.

"I would like to know what two hundred cycles of that does to a population. I expect the honest answer is that nobody has asked."
notes: Both answers are honest and neither is a trap - what he wants is a fact he could not have got from a document.

text:
"Commander. I have spent the layover reading Jangala's export schedule, which I accept is not what an observation deck is for."

He has it open anyway.

"Feedstock, food products, xenobiological stock nobody else in the Sector can supply. Most Luddic sects hold the world sacred. The Hegemony has kept a garrison over it since forever."

"Fifty cycles of that, and the farms are still farms."

He looks up.

"How is that done? Not the doctrine - I have the doctrine, it runs to four pages and says nothing useful. The procedure. Somebody holds a world that does not want them and does not shell it. I want to know what that looks like from the inside. Because in my experience it looks like ordnance."
notes: Hegemony thread, the heaviest of the four - his own war asked as a procurement question. Queued on docking at Jangala.

options: 10:korrin_heg_jang_reports:They shell it, you haven't read those reports
11:korrin_heg_jang_supply:They need the harvest more than they need the obedience
12:korrin_heg_jang_luddics:Luddites, they'd fold at the first orbital strike anyway

text:
"Then I would like to read them, and I notice nobody has offered."

He writes the request down regardless.

"A garrison that shells a holy world every twenty cycles and files it as a pacification is a thing I understand. It is what we did, in better weather."

"What I cannot understand is a garrison that does not. That is the version I came here hoping to find."

"Then it is not restraint. It is a supply line."

"I guess restraint is a decision somebody has to keep making every morning, and mornings change. A supply line has to be replaced before anybody can afford to change their mind about it."

He writes it down.

"I have spent a long time looking for the moral difference between one thing and another. It may only ever have been a freight schedule."
notes: The answer that lands. He reads freight manifests for pleasure - the conclusion arrives in the vocabulary he actually thinks in.

text:
"They have held a growing season through fifty cycles of martial law. Folding is not the word."

He does not raise his voice, and he does not let it go either.

"The last people described to me in that tone were on Ring-Port. The assessment on my desk said one serious push. It took eleven months, and I was the push."

"Contempt gets the timing wrong, Commander. That is the only thing I have ever seen it do."
notes: TRAP - contempt for a population. He refuses the premise in specifics rather than withdrawing. Terminal.

text:
He has the docking register open, and has gone a good deal further into it than berthing requires.

"Ninety-one hulls parked out there that nobody intends to use this cycle. Some are queued for refit. Some are queued for the tow to Arcadia and the breakers. Several are queued for both, in that order, and have been since before I was born."

He continues to scroll.

"The Alliance has never once had a hull it could afford to leave parked. Everything we own is flying, or used as parts for something that will."

He stops on an entry.

"The dockmaster told me this complex is traditionally commanded by a senior officer at the end of his usefulness. There is a posting here for a man who has stopped being needed... We do not have those."
notes: Hegemony thread. An August question asked about somebody else's navy - queued on docking at Ragnar Complex.

options: 10:korrin_heg_rag_sack:It's where they put the officers they can't sack

text:
"That's what I said, the dockmaster corrected me."

"He said it is where they put the officers they do not have to sack. He thought the distinction was obvious, and I have been chewing on it since."

He writes it down.

"An institution with somewhere to put its old men never has to decide anything about them. That is either mercy or a filing system. I would want to see the pension schedule before I said which."

"Yes."

No hedging, and no attempt to make it a smaller question than it is.

"August is old. He has been old for a long time and everybody has agreed not to notice. There is no Ragnar in Fafnir. No complex to be sent to, no schedule, no berth - there is the post. And there is whatever happens when he is no longer in it."

He closes the register.

"The second one is not written down anywhere. I have looked, Commander. Finding that sort of thing is what I am good at, and it is not there."
notes: Feeds the august and succession casual topics without spending either. Ungated deliberately - the option reads fine to a player who has not opened those.

text:
He is reading something he has printed onto paper, which he does not often bother to do.

"Coatl runs the Aztlan command's training. The syllabus is posted in the concourse on a board where anybody can read it. I stood in front of it for twenty minutes and nobody asked me why."

He indicates a line partway down the sheet.

"AI compliance inspection. Three weeks. It sits between customs procedure and small-craft boarding, and the same rated crews rotate through the three."

He sets the sheet down.

"I have spent my working life, like most in my line of work, afraid of this system. So tell me what the procedure actually is. Either we have been a great deal safer than I was told, or we have been lucky for fifty cycles. I would like to know which one I am living in."
notes: Hegemony thread. Answers the question he asks in the sector casual topic - do they actually inspect. Queued on docking at Coatl.

options: 10:korrin_heg_coatl_works:Anything with a core in it gets found

text:
"Then we have not been lucky. We have been covered."

He does not look pleased to have arrived there.

"Cover is a thing somebody provides, and nobody has ever provided it out of good feeling. Somebody is paying. I do not know the currency, and I have exactly enough clearance to know that I am not cleared for it."

"I would rather have been lucky."
notes: Points at the Tri-Tachyon arrangement without naming it. He has not been told and cannot be.

text:
"So the thing keeping the Alliance alive is that we are not interesting."

He enjoys that, and then visibly dislikes enjoying it.

"I think I am pretty good at being uninteresting, making things look uninteresting. I have always thought of it as a personal eccentricity."

He folds the sheet into his coat.

"It appears to also be the strategic posture."

A soft laugh follows.

"Nobody has ever mentioned that I was doing foreign policy."
notes: Lands on his blind spot from the other side - being uninteresting as survival, at both scales.

text:
He is turning a cup of something gone cold over in both hands, not drinking it.

"Commander. I have been on that concourse for two hours and I have not written a single thing down."

"There is a battlestation over this rock at its heaviest rating, a garrison on the surface under it, and heavy batteries between the two. That is not how a company defends a factory. It is how a state defends a border."

He sets the cup down without having drunk any of it.

"So I have one question I am comfortable asking on this deck. Who is it for? Who do they actually expect."
notes: Tri-Tachyon thread opener. The register is careful rather than curious - he has a guess he has never filed, and the cold cup standing in for the notes he never took is the tell. Queued by KorrinObserver on docking at Culann.

text:
"Then they are the only people in the Sector who have built for the war they are actually in."

He turns that over for a moment.

"The Hegemony wants what is done here stopped and cannot afford to say so plainly. So it stays a customs matter until the day it stops being one. Everybody involved knows that day is coming. Nobody will be the first to put a date on it."

He looks up at the fortress arms, briefly.

"I have spent my working life inside that arrangement without once seeing it from the outside. It is a great deal uglier from here."

"The price is remarkably high and nobody appears to have complained about it."

He looks along the berthing arms for longer than the answer needs.

"A company that keeps a fleet, a garrison and a fortress has not bought protection. It has stopped needing to buy any. There ought to be a word for that."

A beat and a moment.

"They are not hiding what they are. They file it under a different heading, and everybody has agreed to read the heading."

"We are standing on their deck, breathing air they sell, under a fortress they built. I have a guess. I have had it a long time and I have never once put it into a document. That is not caution - that is the whole of my professional life in a single decision."

He takes out his slate, opens it, and begins recording the berthing charges. He has not touched it all afternoon.

"You may raise it again in Fafnir if you want to, Commander. Not here."
notes: TRAP - pushing him to say it out loud on a Tri-Tachyon deck. He refuses in specifics and retreats into clerk behaviour, which is the legible loss: the document comes back out. Terminal. Do not write a version where he lands it.

text:
He has the port's general declaration schedule open. It is one page. He turns it over to check, and it is still one page.

"Commander. I have spent the layover trying to buy a copy of the customs tariff for this port. I have been told - politely, four separate times - that there is not one."

He appears torn between delight and something considerably less comfortable.

"I knew the term. I did not understand it until I stood in a megaport and watched a bonded hauler declare eleven thousand tonnes as goods."

He turns the schedule over once more, as if it might have grown a second page.

"This is the first place I have been where nobody bothers with the telling. So who reads anything here? A port this size does not run on trust. I would like to know where the actual record is kept."
notes: Tri-Tachyon thread. The manifest man in the one port that has abolished the manifest. Queued on docking at Eochu Bres.

text:
"Of course."

He says it the way a man does when he has been holding something the wrong way round for an hour.

"It is not an absence of records. It is a monopoly on them. Every party here is unaudited by everybody except the one that owns the floor they are standing on."

"That is a better instrument than ours by a considerable margin. Ours requires people to be careful. Theirs only requires them to be somewhere."

"Then discretion is the commodity and the freight is incidental."

He watches the traffic on the concourse for a while, counting something.

"My career has been treating secrecy as a cost. A thing you pay in order to keep something. Here it is stock. It sits on a shelf, it has a price, and somebody is running a margin on it."

"I do not yet know why that unsettles me more than the alternative did."

"I found it in ninety minutes and it cost me one drink."

He is pleased about this and makes no attempt to hide it.

"Berth assignments, mass on and mass off, hull registries where the crew could be bothered. Nobody is concealing any of it because nobody has ever asked. A free port is not a port without records. It is a port where the records are dull enough that no one reads them."

He almost smiles.

"That is the most reassuring thing I have learned since leaving Fafnir. I am extremely employable here."
notes: The funny one, and the one that most sounds like him. His method works better here than at home, which he finds restful and does not examine.

text:
He has a labor schedule open - a roster of shifts and terms, which is a document he has been asking three separate offices for since you docked.

"Commander. Very nearly everybody on this rock is here on a contract with an end date printed on it."

He scrolls.

"High gravity, tectonic activity, no atmosphere, and ore in quantities that would fund the Alliance twice over. A company does not settle a world like this. It rotates people through it."

He looks up.

"So I would like to know what the end date means in practice. When a contract runs out on Tibicena, where does the person actually go? There is a berth home written into the terms - I have read the terms. What I want to know is whether anybody takes it."
notes: Tri-Tachyon thread, and the personal one. His grandparents were contract labour off-world on the day their state stopped existing; the third option reaches that without him volunteering it. Queued on docking at Tibicena.

options: 10:korrin_tt_tib_renew:They re-sign. There is nothing to go back to
11:korrin_tt_tib_home:Most take the berth. It is a job, not a life
12:korrin_tt_tib_why:Why does the last clause matter so much to you?

text:
"So the end date is decoration?"

He does not sound surprised. He does not sound satisfied either.

"A term nobody exercises is not a term. It is a description of the place people are already living, written in the tense of somewhere they are going to leave."

He closes the schedule.

"I would want the second-generation figures. If there are children on this rock who were born to a rotation, the company has founded a colony and filed it as staffing. Somebody ought to tell them. I do not believe they have noticed."

"Good, I think."

"Then it is work. Hard work at a bad address, which is an ordinary thing, and I have read a great deal this cycle that was not."

He thinks for a brief second.

"I would still like to know how many go and how many are back inside the same cycle. A berth home you use twice is a commute, and that is a different arrangement entirely. Nobody's paperwork would show the difference."

"My grandparents were contract labor off-world."

He says it the way you would give somebody an address.

"A rotation on Tiamat, with a berth home written into the terms. They were most of a year into it when their home stopped existing. Nobody canceled the contract. There was simply nowhere left for the last clause to send them."

He puts the schedule away.

"So when I am handed one of these I read the end of it first and the fine print. It's the only part of the document that matters."
notes: Reaches the stranded-descent material through somebody else's paperwork. He states the fact and lets the player do the arithmetic - no confession, and no sympathy offered.

text:
He has been reading a recruitment board, which on Port Tse is a physical board with physical paper on it.

"Commander. Four captains are advertising here today. Two of them list previous employers by name."

He indicates one of the sheets.

text: "Cold. Not dramatically - just always, in a way you stop mentioning after the first winter." He goes through the motions of paperwork he does not have. "Third shift meant everyone interesting was asleep and everyone tedious was awake. I got very good at my job because there was nothing else to do with the hours."

"Different, not better. Ring-Port asked more of me and told me less. Kori told me everything and asked almost nothing." He considers it seriously. "I have never worked out which one I would recommend to somebody."

He does not deflect it.

"It was, some nights. I read to fill them, and then I was good at reading, and then that was the job. I am not sure which came first, and it does not especially matter now."

"Not much, and I mean that as a compliment to whoever runs it." He glances at a manifest that has nothing to do with the question.

"Gravity assist for half the traffic in this system, and a mining operation on the moons that has never once made an incident log. I have started to suspect boring is a skill, and that somebody at Vorium is unusually good at it."

text:
"Ore pulled straight from the cooled magma chambers. High-grade, and hot enough on extraction that the safety numbers were their own small argument every rotation."

He states it without weight.

"It was work. I do not have more to give it than that, and I would be inventing something if I tried."

"Still running."

"I checked, obviously. Alliance-operated now, same ore, better numbers than the ones I mentioned. I do not know why that mattered to confirm, only that it did."

"Sensor stations, watching a star that has not done anything unusual in five billion years."

He says it entirely straight.

"I asked why we still crew the maintenance runs, and the answer I got was 'in case it does.' - but that wasn't entirely true, we don't actually have any people stationed there anymore, yet the sensors are maintained all the same"
"It is the correct answer." He allows a beat for it. "That does not make it a satisfying one."
"It is. I priced the maintenance schedule once, out of curiosity, and then wished I had not."
"Close enough to log it. Not close enough to see anything the sensors had not already told me twice."

"Enormously. I have read the storm data."

He is entirely serious about this.

"You should be too, and you are welcome for the recommendation."

"None, professionally."

He shrugs it off easily.

"Every ship in this system uses it to know which way is home. That is the whole appeal, and it is a better one than most things get."

"A rotating crew of four. Six-month postings, minimal contact."

He says it as a fact he has looked at more than once.

"I considered volunteering for it, before Ring-Port came up."

"The quiet, mostly."

He answers it honestly.

"I have never minded my own company. There is something to be said for a job where the only person who can find fault with your work is yourself."

"So am I, on balance."

He says it lightly, and means it.

"Though I would have made an excellent hermit, and I stand by that."

text:
"Well you've read the logs." A measured pause. "You know more than most officers who've served under me."

A silence. You hear something - keys, or equipment - before he continues.

"Certain precautions are required for this channel, given what we're discussing."

"The brief the Office gave me and what the Office actually knows are not the same document. I'll tell you what I can. Which is less than you'll want."

"Good." A brief pause. "And Commander - the Alliance doesn't forget the people who handle information correctly. Safe travels."

text:
"Because the Gate was never the source." A pause. "The pings stopped the moment we cracked Kori's surface. Whatever was responding - it didn't come through gates. It was already here."

The encryption holds. He doesn't move.

"The Gate was a receiver. A way of asking whether something was listening. Once we understood that, continuing at the Gate was redundant. The conversation had already moved."

"I gave them a mandate and they filled it." His tone lays flat. No defensiveness. "Counterintelligence. Then signals. Then guarding Kori. Each expansion seemed reasonable at the time, inside the emergency we were managing."

A brief silence.

"By the time I understood what they'd become, reversing it would have required options I no longer had. The Office knows too much. The Office does too much. And the Alliance depends on both." He pauses. "Some blindspots are chosen, Commander. You'll learn that if you haven't already."

"Our key to survival." A pause. "That's what I told myself."

He shifts. The encryption distorts around the motion.

"A Domain-era computational device. Designated LONGSIGHT. Built to coordinate colonial infrastructure across multiple systems - resource allocation, logistics, production planning. Never finished. Sealed when the Collapse severed its purpose."

He is quiet for a moment.

"Then the Office woke it." Another pause, heavier. "And that's where the fog of war begins. I know the outline. The Office knows the rest."

The line is quiet for a moment. Longer than it needs to be.

"You've heard more than most, Commander." His voice is measured and deliberate. "Let me ask you something in return."

A pause.

"Given everything you know - the Gate, Kori, the Office, what was necessary to keep this system alive - what would you have done in my position?"
options:
1:gate_logs_ans_same:I would've done the same as you

text:
"I'm so surrounded by yes-men that it is hard to believe it, but given the benefit of doubt."

He is still for a moment.

"Good..." The word lands without inflection. "That's the correct answer, and the honest one."

A pause.

"Survival doesn't come with clean choices. Anyone who tells you otherwise has never been responsible for something that cannot be allowed to fail."

"I'm glad we understand each other."

"Yes." He doesn't dismiss it. "You might have."

A pause.

"I've had that thought myself. In the years after Kori went active - what might we have learned, if we'd moved more slowly. If we'd been less desperate."

The encrypted silhouette is still.

"But the war didn't give us time for philosophy, Commander. It rarely does. We understood enough to survive. I'm not certain understanding more would have made us safer."

"Neither would I." The voice is dry. "In principle. The problem with principle is that it requires you to identify the line before you've crossed it."

A pause.

"The Office was useful. Then it was necessary. Then it was irreplaceable. Each transition seemed logical at the time. The war makes everything seem logical." He is quiet for a moment. "If you find a way to draw that line clearly, Commander, let me know. I've been looking for it for thirty years."

He stares at you for a moment. Then he laughs.

Brief. Unguarded. He doesn't appear to have expected it any more than you did.

A pause.

The silence that follows is almost thoughtful.

"...Right."

He moves on as if it didn't happen.

"Good." A pause. "That's a more honest answer than most."

He is quiet.

"Neither did I, at the time. That's the truth of it. The Gate responded, and we followed the thread because we were losing and we needed anything we could use. And we accepted it because the alternative was starvation and slow defeat." The encrypted silhouette is still. "I made decisions under uncertainty and they kept the Alliance alive. I don't know if they were right. But I know they were necessary."

A brief pause.

"That distinction gets heavier every year."

"Likewise, Commander."

He keys something. The encrypted image holds for a moment, then clears.

"We'll be in touch."

The link closes.

You walk the rest of the way in, past machinery clearly older than the Alliance itself.

The room is small, spare, and cold - its convenience for humans was never the point. A woman is standing at the far end of it, reading something off a data-slate that she doesn't care to look up from until you've stopped moving.

She sets the slate down without finishing whatever was on it. "What an honor." She is difficult to read, but you get the feeling she does not mean this as a form of flattery.
notes: Monroe's own opening, split out of the original XLII_monroe_vetting_open so Ancker's escort scene could be inserted ahead of it. text:
"I am Haspel Monroe. I run the Office - and not the arm of it you've dealt with, nor the one that occasionally embarrasses itself in front of Tri-Tachyon. I am the sum of it all."

She tilts her head ever so slightly and gives the faintest impression of a cruel smile.

"August and I have never really seen eye to eye, except for you. He wants to hand you a piece of something this Alliance has spent years keeping off every ledger. He's given you a recommendation for something particularly old - but in the end that decision comes down to me."
notes: Second half of Monroe's opening, continuing from XLII_monroe_vetting_begin's Continue option. Carries the FireAll XLII_MonroeQAMenu that used to live on the begin row, so the Q&A options only appear once she's actually finished talking.

text:
"Because rank answers to whoever's alive to give the order."

She checks the slate again without reading it, more habit than attention.

"Continuity answers to whoever planned past that point. August didn't. I did. But to enunciate more clearly, the Alliance answers to the Office, one way or another."

"Let's call it a disused observation post, a gift from our friends on the other side."

A faint, humorless precision on the word disused.

"It has simply never needed anyone outside this room to know otherwise."

"I've read what August sent, and I've read what he didn't think to send."

She studies you the way she studies a report she's already decided on. "You're reliable enough for what he wants to give you. I'm not asking whether you agree with that. I'm telling you I've already decided it."

A pause that costs her exactly as much as it costs her to spend it, then it's gone. "What you will be handed answers to questions you haven't been given yet. Don't go looking for them. When the Alliance needs you to have them, you will."

She's already reaching for the slate again, done with you before she says so.

"Tell August his something is cleared. He'll know what that means. He'll have work for you."

"Then we understand each other." The encrypted silhouette leans forward slightly.

"To cut the ceremony, we are looking for a pristine condition Nanoforge. Which yes, I understand the gravity of our request, but I assure you I would entrust this to no one else.

"Bring it to me directly. I won't ask where you found it. You won't need to ask what we intend to do with it."

He doesn't wait for you to answer before he continues, already treating it as settled.

"The Alliance, nor I, forget its debts, Commander."

The silhouette on the screen is still for a long moment.

"Some things are better kept off the record. But thank you, truly."

You hear something being keyed in the background.

"The forge goes to Kori. What it will do will outlast us both."

A pause - the first one that doesn't feel like calculated investigation of you.

"There's a second matter. It isn't ready to hand over yet." He doesn't say when it will be. "You won't hear it from me first, when it comes. I'd get used to that, if I were you."

"Needless to say, this stays between us until then, Commander."

Threshold corrected (author feedback, later session, from live testing): was 400, derived from the wrong gate entirely. The 5%-effectiveness floor (VALUABLES_THRESHOLD) that merely enables "Designate raid objectives" barely moves with $raidDifficulty and was never the real constraint. The actual number is CustomRaidObjective.marinesRequired, set from AddRaidObjective's EXTREME danger tier (RaidDangerLevel.EXTREME.marineTokens = 7 out of MAX_MARINE_TOKENS = 10, MarketCMD.java) and converted into an actual marine count by the raid picker's native UI via getMarinesFor(): marines = tokens * RE_PER_MARINE_TOKEN * defenderStr / (1 - tokens * RE_PER_MARINE_TOKEN) = (7/3) * $raidDifficulty. That's confirmed by live play - the raid actually needed "closer to 14000" marines at the old $raidDifficulty=7000, matching this formula's ~16,300 prediction far better than the old 5%-floor math's ~368. See XLII_burn_raid_setup's own notes for the full derivation and the $raidDifficulty retune (7000 -> 2571, targeting ~6000 marines required) that came out of the same investigation. 6000 here matches that target exactly - if $raidDifficulty changes again, recompute this threshold as (7/3) * raidDifficulty, not the old VALUABLES_THRESHOLD-based formula.
